cue: Wave one hand side to side (Hello / Hi)
description: The robot raises its arm to a visible waving position, then performs a repetitive, friendly side-to-side motion with its gripper, resembling a human wave.
reasoning:
# Q1: A human wave reads best when the hand is already visible and then performs a repeated side-to-side accent.
# Q2: candidates=P1) up+horizontal+x60,y50,z65, P2) front+horizontal+x70,y50,z60, P3) back+horizontal+x55,y50,z60; winner=P1 because the raised horizontal hand gives the clearest waving silhouette before the wrist motion begins, while front/back look more like presenting than greeting.
# Q3: options=M1 P1>movement(wrist y repeat), M2 P1>path(line y), M3 P2>movement(elbow y repeat); winner=M1 because waving is inherently repetitive local articulation, so a wrist-led repeated movement preserves the greeting read better than a path sweep or a larger elbow swing.

# Q2: candidates=P1) up+horizontal+x50,y50,z50, P2) right+vertical+x50,y100,z50, P3) up+vertical+x50,y75,z70; winner=P1 because it provides a neutral setup that makes the later forehead approach and fold readable, while jumping straight to the side or high forehead pose loses the staged construction of the salute.

description: The robot moves its hand deliberately to one eye, performs a gentle rubbing motion to convey tiredness, and then slowly retracts its arm with a lingering sense of fatigue.
planning_shot:
Visualization: The robot raises its hand to one eye, lightly rubs it, and lowers away with a tired lingering finish.
Iconic pose: The hand clearly covering or touching one eye.
Recognition anchor: Direct placement at the eye region followed by small local rubbing.
Motion read: The viewer should read tiredness quickly from the eye-targeted reach and rub.
Pre-action reveal: Reach to the eye first before any rubbing begins.
Why this example matters: Tired fails when the motion becomes generic midair oscillation instead of a specific eye rub.
reasoning:
# Q1: Tiredness reads when the hand reaches the eye first and then performs a small local rub instead of a generic midair wiggle.
# Q2: candidates=P1) left+vertical+x70,y55,z40, P2) front+horizontal+x55,y50,z65, P3) back+vertical+x45,y50,z55; winner=P1 because the lateral vertical hand best simulates direct eye contact, while front/back placements weaken the specific eye-rub analogy.
# Q3: options=M1 P1>movement(wrist y repeat), M2 P1>path(arc yz), M3 P2>movement(elbow y repeat); winner=M1 because tiredness is conveyed by small repeated local rubbing after the hand reaches the eye, and wrist repetition preserves that read better than a larger arc.

description: The robot first reveals a clean, slightly off-center 'face' presentation so the viewer can read the head area, then performs a cute side tilt that clearly favors one side, holds that tilted silhouette for a beat, and eases out with a tiny lingering inquisitive adjustment.

Iconic pose: A clearly side-tilted head-like silhouette, held for a beat.
Recognition anchor: The gripper/head region must visibly lean left or right, not just wobble generically.
Motion read: Within the first second, the viewer should read 'curious head tilt,' not just 'small movement.'
Pre-action reveal: Present the head area slightly forward and to one side before the tilt, so the tilt has a clear baseline.
Why this example matters: Curiosity fails when the tilt is too subtle or when the motion reads as generic fidgeting.
reasoning:
# Q1: Curiosity reads as a visible head-like presentation followed by a small but clearly biased side tilt that is held briefly.
# Q2: candidates=P1) front+horizontal+x58,y48,z58, P2) left+horizontal+x55,y40,z60, P3) up+vertical+x50,y50,z70; winner=P1 because it gives the cleanest neutral face-like baseline before the tilt, while side or upward anchors make the later lean less interpretable as a head tilt.
# Q3: options=M1 P1>movement(elbow y hold), M2 P1>path(line y), M3 P2>movement(wrist y repeat); winner=M1 because curiosity depends on a single held tilt, not a repeated wag or explicit path trace, so one elbow-led lean with a hold is the clearest structure.

cue: Bow slightly from the waist (Respect / Greeting)
description: The robot settles into a modest chest-height stance, then performs a single coupled forward-and-downward bow, holds the respectful lowered line briefly, and rises back up without extra flourish.
planning_shot:
Visualization: The robot gives a restrained, polite bow with one clean dip and a readable hold at the lowest point.
Iconic pose: A visibly lowered respectful torso line, not just a generic forward pitch.
Recognition anchor: The bow should read as both forward and downward at the same time, so the arm silhouette clearly dips.
Motion read: The viewer should immediately read a polite bow rather than a loose shoulder swing.
Pre-action reveal: Establish a simple upright baseline pose before the coupled bow begins.
Why this example matters: Bow fails when only one axis changes and the motion reads like a generic pitch instead of a respectful dip.
reasoning:
# Q1: A respectful bow reads when an upright baseline is followed by one coupled forward-and-downward dip with a short hold at the lowest point.
# Q2: candidates=P1) down+vertical+x48,y50,z45, P2) front+horizontal+x55,y50,z50, P3) back+vertical+x40,y50,z40; winner=P1 because the downward vertical stance sets up a respectful torso-like line that makes the later coupled dip readable, whereas front/back anchors look more like offering or retraction.
# Q3: options=M1 P1>movement(shoulder x+z dip and return), M2 P1>path(line x), M3 P2>movement(shoulder z only); winner=M1 because a bow is defined by a coupled forward-and-downward dip, and splitting or simplifying the axes weakens the respectful read.
